question: Your Agent SDK developer tool has a coordinator and four subagents: an explorer subagent, a generator subagent, a documentation writer subagent, and an automation subagent. Before a release, you audit the allowedTools configuration of each subagent. Which two findings show scoped tool access applied correctly?

options.text: The documentation writer subagent has Bash so that it can run full test suites to confirm the behavior that it documents.
options.reason: Running test suites is outside the documentation role, and agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them.

options.text: The documentation writer subagent still has the schema migration tools of the database MCP server, which it needed once for a rare task last quarter.
options.reason: Cross-role tools are for specific high-frequency needs, so tools for a rare past task are outside the role and add selection complexity.

options.text: The automation subagent receives every tool from all four connected MCP servers, so that engineers can give it any repetitive task without first changing its configuration.
options.reason: Giving an agent many tools beyond its role degrades tool selection reliability, and scoped access gives only the tools that the role needs.

options.text: The explorer subagent has only Read, Grep, and Glob in its allowedTools, because its role is to search and read code.
options.reason: Scoped tool access gives an agent only the tools that its role needs, and searching and reading code needs only these tools.

options.text: The generator subagent has one read-only get_naming_rule tool from the documentation domain, because it checks a naming rule for almost every file it generates.
options.reason: Scoped tool access allows limited cross-role tools for specific high-frequency needs, and this tool is narrow and serves a need that occurs on almost every file.
